title: The Uncomfortable Truth
content:
The conference room was almost empty when Clara found Daniel standing beside the window, staring at the city below. The meeting had ended twenty minutes earlier, but neither of them had left. On the table, several documents remained scattered beside two untouched cups of coffee.

—You knew about the report, didn't you? —Clara asked.

Daniel did not turn around immediately.

—I knew there was a report.

—That's not what I asked.

—I suppose it isn't.

Clara picked up one of the documents and glanced at the highlighted sections.

—These figures were deliberately omitted from the presentation.

—Yes.

—And you approved the presentation.

—I did.

She placed the document back on the table.

—Then explain something to me. How can you approve a report that conceals information you know is fundamental to the decision we're supposed to make?

Daniel finally turned toward her.

—Because the situation was more complicated than you realize.

—That's precisely the kind of sentence people use when they don't want to provide an explanation.

—I anticipated that reaction.

—Did you anticipate mine?

—Particularly yours.

Clara folded her arms.

—Then you also anticipated that I would consider this a serious breach of professional integrity.

—I did.

—And yet you proceeded.

Daniel sighed.

—I wasn't trying to deceive anyone.

—Intentions don't erase consequences.

—I know.

—Do you?

The question lingered between them.

Daniel walked toward the table and sat down.

—The preliminary data was inconsistent. We had three independent analyses, and none of them produced identical results. If we had included every discrepancy in the presentation, the board would have interpreted the uncertainty as evidence that the entire project was fundamentally defective.

—Perhaps they should have.

—That's easy to say now.

—No, it isn't. It's difficult to say precisely because I understand the implications.

Daniel looked at her carefully.

—You think we should have suspended the project?

—I think we should have disclosed the uncertainty and allowed the board to decide whether the potential benefits justified the risks.

—And if they had rejected it?

—Then we would have accepted their decision.

—Even after three years of work?

—Especially after three years of work.

Daniel leaned back in his chair.

—You realize how many people would have been affected by that decision?

—Of course I do.

—Hundreds of employees, investors, suppliers, researchers. Entire departments have been reorganized around this project.

—That doesn't make the information less relevant.

—It makes the decision more consequential.

—Exactly.

Daniel remained silent for several seconds.

—There's something you don't know.

Clara raised an eyebrow.

—I'm listening.

—The discrepancy wasn't the only problem.

—What else was there?

—One of the external laboratories questioned the reliability of the original methodology.

Clara's expression changed.

—You never mentioned that.

—I couldn't.

—Couldn't, or wouldn't?

Daniel hesitated.

—Wouldn't.

—Why?

—Because the laboratory was contractually bound to confidentiality, and we hadn't yet determined whether their criticism was technically justified.

—So instead of telling the board that the methodology had been challenged, you removed the entire section from the presentation.

—Yes.

Clara walked slowly toward the window.

—That's worse than I thought.

—I know.

—Do you understand what this means?

—Probably better than you think.

—It means the board wasn't making an informed decision.

—I know.

—It means we presented a controlled narrative rather than the complete evidence.

—I know.

—And it means that if someone discovers this later, they'll assume we intentionally manipulated the findings.

Daniel looked down.

—They might be right.

Clara turned toward him.

—Are you admitting that you manipulated the information?

—I'm admitting that I allowed the presentation to become more reassuring than the evidence justified.

—That's a remarkably careful way of putting it.

—I have spent the last two weeks trying to find a less uncomfortable way to describe what happened.

—And?

—There isn't one.

Clara sat opposite him.

—Why didn't you tell me?

—Because I thought you'd stop the project.

—You were right.

—That's why.

—You didn't trust me.

—I trusted your judgment. I was afraid of it.

Clara was silent.

Outside, the city continued moving beneath the glass towers, indifferent to the ethical dispute unfolding several floors above it.

—What happens now? —she finally asked.

Daniel looked at the documents.

—We disclose everything.

—To the board?

—To the board, the research committee, and the external auditors.

—Even if they terminate the project?

—Even then.

Clara studied his face.

—You realize you could lose your position.

—Yes.

—And I could lose mine.

—I know.

—Then why are you suddenly willing to do this?

Daniel stood and gathered the documents into a single stack.

—Because I finally understood something.

—What?

—A project can survive a disappointing result. It can survive a financial loss. It can even survive being cancelled.

He paused.

—What it cannot survive is becoming successful for the wrong reasons.

Clara stared at him for a moment.

—That's the first sensible thing you've said tonight.

Daniel gave a tired smile.

—I'll take that as encouragement.

—Don't.

—Fair enough.

She picked up her coat.

—Send me the complete dataset before midnight.

—I will.

—And Daniel?

—Yes?

—Don't edit anything this time.

He nodded.

—I won't.

Clara reached the door, then stopped.

—You know, admitting that we were wrong isn't the most difficult part.

Daniel looked at her.

—What's the difficult part?

—Accepting that we might have been wrong when everything was going exactly the way we wanted.

She opened the door.

—That's when people become most dangerous.

Daniel watched her leave.

For the first time that evening, he understood that the real problem had never been the numbers.

It had been the temptation to believe that a desirable conclusion was automatically a trustworthy one.
